In Kusaiean the strongest stress within a word falls on the next to the last syllable, also known as the penultimate syllable. This means that the first syllable of two-syllable words receives the strongest stress. Observe the following ... This rule holds true when a word has suffixes attached and the number of syllables increases. Notice how the syllable that carries the primary stress shifts when the word is suffixed. (See 3.2 ... new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Copies checked (1) Lee 1975 Kusaiean Reference Grammar: I re-parsed the raw OpenLibrary search-inside responses myself rather than trusting the extracted. Every hit carries IA identifier kusaieanreferenc0000yiki, creator 'Yi, Ki-dong, 1940-' (= Lee Kee-dong), title 'Kusaiean reference grammar', 1975, University Press of Hawaii, subject 'Kosraean language -- Grammar' -- so the snippets are from the right book and the right languoid (Kusaiean = Kosraean, ISO kos, kosr1238). The snippet sentences quoted by the other reader are present verbatim across the responses: 'STRESS PATTERN.. In Kusaiean the strongest stress within a word falls on the next to the last syllable, also known as the penulti…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the penultimate syllable, counting syllables (not moras); in disyllables the first syllable is stressed; the domain includes suffixes, so stress moves rightward when suffixes add syllables (muhláhlah -> muhlahláhyak).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Lee 1975:33 distinguishes three (or more) degrees of stress, illustrated with trisyllabic kasrkuhsrak 'angered': loudest on the penult kuh, next-strongest on the first syllable kasr, weakest on the final srak; Kennedy 2003:259 summarizes Lee as 'secondary stress on the antepenult'. No fuller alternating rule seen in the accessible snippets.
new_statements.exceptions: None in the accessible text of Lee 1975 p. 33 (pp. 34-35 not seen in full). Lee & Wang 1984:437 n. 22 remark that muhta- 'eye, face' and tuhma- 'father' 'are stressed on the second syllable' with reduced uh in the first syllable; Kennedy 2003:259 notes non-initial vowels are phonetically long, but stress placement ignores weight.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated on citation forms including suffixes (stress shifts with suffixation). Rehg 1984 frames Micronesian penultimate stress as phrase-level generally, but Lee's Kosraean statement is explicitly 'within a word'. Lee 1975 full text (pp. 33-35) was accessible only as search-inside snippets; the sentences quoted are verbatim from those snippets, with [..] marking gaps between snippets.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Kosraean = Kusaiean (older spelling), Glottolog kosr1238, ISO kos; Lee 1975 uses the 1973 Kusaiean Orthography Committee spelling; no dialect restriction stated.
